teaching.causalExplanation: Speed only tells you how fast something's going. Velocity tells you how fast, and which way. Look at the four arrows copied side by side. They're the same length, so the speed is the same, but they point four different ways, so the velocity is different each time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not of speed. So yes, the tip is accelerating, the whole way round. Moving in a circle at a constant speed like this is called uniform circular motion. So which way is the velocity changing? Take two moments a little apart. Copy their velocity arrows so they start from the same point. The change in velocity, delta v, is the arrow that takes you from the tip of the first to the tip of the second. Now bring the two moments closer and closer together. The change ends up pointing straight at the centre of the circle. So the acceleration points towards the centre too. It's called centripetal acceleration, which means centre-seeking, and it's always at right angles to the velocity. To put numbers on this, we need a few ways to describe circular motion. Here's a car going round a circular track of radius fifty metres. It takes twelve seconds to do one lap. That's the period, capital T, the time for one complete revolution. The frequency, f, is the number of revolutions each second, so f equals one over T. We can also describe how fast it turns. An angle in radians is the arc length divided by the radius, so one full lap is two pi radians. Angular velocity, omega, is the angle turned divided by the time taken. For one lap, that's two pi over T.

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How can speed be constant while velocity keeps changing?" The answer, built in order: velocity carries direction, so a turning velocity is a changing velocity (2); the change points to the centre (3); the motion is described by T, f and ω, giving v = 2πr/T = ωr (4 to 6); the velocity arrow's tip goes round its own circle, which gives a = v²/r (7, 8); Newton's second law then needs an inward net force mv²/r (9).
- **Hook (v10 handoff, site hook re-objected).** The site's hook is a car at constant speed on a bend; v10 handed over a slewing crane seen from above, so the question is asked of the jib tip first, then the car takes over for numbers (4 onward), as on the site. Prediction chips "No: its speed is constant" and "Yes", 3 s countdown.
- **Speedometer beat (site "constant speedometer reading").** The dashboard cluster plate (existing) sits small beside the car in scene 4 with its needle still, to make "constant speed" concrete. Needle position is illustrative; no value is read.
- **Δv construction (site card 2 and the "Explain 6 marks" step 4).** Two velocity arrows from nearby moments are copied tail to tail and Δv is drawn from the first tip to the second; the interval then shrinks (40°, 20°, 5°) and Δv swings to aim at the centre. This is the route's "relate displacement of velocity vectors to inward acceleration".
- **Deriving a = v²/r (route entry knowledge: derive each new equation).** The site states a_c = v²/r without derivation. The design uses the velocity-circle argument: with every velocity arrow drawn from one point, the tip moves round a circle of radius v once per period, so the rate of change of velocity is 2πv/T; with T = 2πr/v this gives v²/r. It needs only v = 2πr/T (just taught) and the definition of acceleration. Similar triangles were considered and rejected (two diagrams and a small-angle limit in one scene). See author note (a).
- **Worked example (site worked examples 1 and 2, unchanged numbers).** r = 50 m, T = 12 s: v = 26.2 m s⁻¹, ω = 0.524 rad s⁻¹, f = 0.0833 Hz, a_c = 13.7 m s⁻² towards the centre. - **v = ωr with the crane (site "outer edge of a spinning DVD").** Two points on the jib, 15 m and 30 m out, sweep the same angle in the same time; the outer arc is twice as long. Qualitative ("twice as far out, twice as fast"); no crane slewing rate is narrated (author note b).
- **Force (site card 3, route `derive-radial-force`).** F_net = ma, so F_net = mv²/r towards the centre. "Centripetal force" is a name for the job done by real forces (site misconception 2 and the "Explain 6 marks" step 5). No numerical force here: the site's worked example 3 (1200 kg car, friction) is v12's opening case, and every real case has at least two forces (route stop).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How can speed be constant while velocity keeps changing?" The answer, built in order: velocity carries direction, so a turning velocity is a changing velocity (2); the change points to the centre (3); the motion is described by T, f and ω, giving v = 2πr/T = ωr (4 to 6); the velocity arrow's tip goes round its own circle, which gives a = v²/r (7, 8); Newton's second law then needs an inward net force mv²/r (9).
- **Hook (v10 handoff, site hook re-objected).** The site's hook is a car at constant speed on a bend; v10 handed over a slewing crane seen from above, so the question is asked of the jib tip first, then the car takes over for numbers (4 onward), as on the site. Prediction chips "No: its speed is constant" and "Yes", 3 s countdown.
- **Speedometer beat (site "constant speedometer reading").** The dashboard cluster plate (existing) sits small beside the car in scene 4 with its needle still, to make "constant speed" concrete. Needle position is illustrative; no value is read.
- **Δv construction (site card 2 and the "Explain 6 marks" step 4).** Two velocity arrows from nearby moments are copied tail to tail and Δv is drawn from the first tip to the second; the interval then shrinks (40°, 20°, 5°) and Δv swings to aim at the centre. This is the route's "relate displacement of velocity vectors to inward acceleration".
- **Deriving a = v²/r (route entry knowledge: derive each new equation).** The site states a_c = v²/r without derivation. The design uses the velocity-circle argument: with every velocity arrow drawn from one point, the tip moves round a circle of radius v once per period, so the rate of change of velocity is 2πv/T; with T = 2πr/v this gives v²/r. It needs only v = 2πr/T (just taught) and the definition of acceleration. Similar triangles were considered and rejected (two diagrams and a small-angle limit in one scene). See author note (a).
- **Worked example (site worked examples 1 and 2, unchanged numbers).** r = 50 m, T = 12 s: v = 26.2 m s⁻¹, ω = 0.524 rad s⁻¹, f = 0.0833 Hz, a_c = 13.7 m s⁻² towards the centre. Three significant figures as the site gives. The car's v is carried unrounded (26.18 m s⁻¹) into a_c; 26.2²/50 = 13.73 also rounds to 13.7.
- **v = ωr with the crane (site "outer edge of a spinning DVD").** Two points on the jib, 15 m and 30 m out, sweep the same angle in the same time; the outer arc is twice as long. Qualitative ("twice as far out, twice as fast"); no crane slewing rate is narrated (author note b).

"Centripetal force" is a name for the job done by real forces (site misconception 2 and the "Explain 6 marks" step 5). scenes.teachingReason: So which way is the velocity changing? Take two moments a little apart. Copy their velocity arrows so they start from the same point. scenes.teachingReason: To put numbers on this, we need a few ways to describe circular motion. Here's a car going round a circular track of radius fifty metres. It takes twelve seconds to do one lap. That's the period, capital T, the time for one complete revolution. The frequency, f, is the number of revolutions each second, so f equals one over T. We can also describe how fast it turns. An angle in radians is the arc length divided by the radius, so one full lap is two pi radians. Angular velocity, omega, is the angle turned divided by the time taken. For one lap, that's two pi over T.

scenes.teachingReason: Newton's second law says the net force points the same way as the acceleration. So anything in uniform circular motion needs a net force pointing towards the centre, of size m v squared over r. This is called the centripetal force. But it isn't a new kind of force. It's just a name for a job that real forces do, the overall push or pull towards the centre. Tension, friction, gravity or a normal force can do that job, on their own or together.

scenes.teachingReason: A common idea is that things moving in a circle get flung outwards. Picture a steel ball on a smooth table, kept in a circle by a string tied to a peg. Now cut the string. With no net force, the ball keeps the velocity it had at that instant, and it moves off in a straight line along the tangent, the line that just touches the circle. It doesn't fly straight out from the centre. Nothing was ever pushing it outwards. The string was only ever pulling it in.

scenes.teachingReason: Four revolutions per second means omega is two pi times four point zero, about twenty-five point one radians per second. The rim speed is omega r, twenty-five point one times zero point three zero, about seven point five metres per second. And a is v squared over r, about one hundred and ninety metres per second squared. The classic slip is writing omega as four, but four is the frequency in hertz, not the angle per second.
